newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CBA PROFITS SEEN SLOWING, EYES ON BUY-BACK.
newsitem.headline: CBA PROFITS SEEN SLOWING, EYES ON BUY-BACK.

text.p: Commonwealth Bank of Australia is expected to report on Wednesday that increasingly tight lending margins flattened profits in the second half of its financial year, analysts said.

But Australia's largest home mortgage lender is expected to sweeten the result announcement with plans for either a share buy-back or a special dividend to return about A$1 billion of excess capital to shareholders, the analysts said.
"There are expectations of a special dividend later in the year, hopefully to be announced on Wednesday," said ABN AMRO Hoare Govett banking analyst Mike Pulman said.

"I'm looking for some form of capital return -- they've got A$1 billion of excess capital," said another senior banking analyst, pointing to either a five percent buy-back or a 70 or 80 cent fully franked special dividend.
Analysts on average forecast CBA's net profit for the year ended June 30 would rise 6.3 percent to A$1.189 billion, BZW's Barceps survey of 15 analysts showed.
Most expect the final dividend to rise to about 55 or 56 cents per share from 52 cents, taking the total dividend to about A$1.00 per share.
But most of this expected profit rise had already been built through the 11 percent rise in first half year profits reported in February.

Second half profits are forecast to have been basically flat at A$587 million, down slightly from A$602 million in the first half and up slightly from the A$577 reported in the second half of 1995/96.
"The main factors to watch are the margin pressure and hopefully cost control," said ABN AMRO's Pulman.

CBA cut its key variable mortgage rate by 145 basis points in the second half while the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) cut its official cash rate by 100 basis points, implying a 45 point margin squeeze in the half.
CBA led the major banks in cutting mortgage rates by 225 basis points in the first half of the 1996/97 year while the RBA cut official rates by 150 basis points, implying a 75 basis point squeeze.
But 75 basis points of the second half cuts did not take effect for existing customers before the end of the half on June 30.
Analysts said this would cushion somewhat the margin squeeze effect in the second half, because banks passed on the official rate cuts to depositers before home lenders.

Analysts expect the effects of the last year's total home mortgage margin squeeze of 120 basis points will hit home in the 1997/98 year for CBA and at the end of the year to September 30 for the three other major banks.
Analysts expect CBA to generate a flat profit at best in 1997/98 unless it can cut costs substantially or significantly boost fee income.
Meanwhile analysts expect the special dividend or buy-back to soften the blow of a flat profit outlook.

CBA had a tier one capital ratio of about 8.8 percent at the end of June 1996, well above the six to seven percent many other major banks operate on and well above the four percent minimum specified by the Reserve Bank.

Some analysts said CBA would prefer a buy-back to a special dividend as it could help smooth the turbulence expected in mid-November when owners of CBA's instalment receipts have to pay the balance owed to the government to take full possession of the shares.
"They'll use a buy-back to finess their share price," said one banking analyst.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
